title: Antigonid Dynasty
capsule: The Antigonid dynasty descended from Antigonus I Monophthalmus ('One-Eye'), one of Alexander the Great's most powerful successors (diadochi), who assumed the royal title in 306 BCE and was killed at the Battle of Ipsus in 301 BCE. His son Demetrius I Poliorcetes briefly seized Macedonia in 294 BCE, establishing the Antigonids as its ruling house; Antigonus II Gonatas consolidated control after defeating the Galatian invasion at the Battle of Lysimachia c. 277 BCE. The dynasty governed Macedonia as a Hellenistic monarchy, balancing relations with the Achaean and Aetolian leagues and resisting Roman expansion until Perseus, the last Antigonid king, was defeated at the Battle of Pydna in 168 BCE, after which Macedonia was divided into four Roman-supervised republics.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. Macedonia's core territory is well attested, but the Antigonids' fluctuating control over Thessaly, Corinth, and Aegean island dependencies is variable and debated; the dataset window (c. 291–277 BCE) captures the turbulent founding period.
